steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on neuron activation coverage (NAC) as a lens on out-of-distribution problems. It should explain the OOD problem and the two lines of work (detection and generalization), why neuron behavior matters and where prior neuron-based methods fall short, how we define NAC, and how we apply it to OOD detection and OOD generalization, with headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- The in-distribution assumption and the OOD problem
- Two avenues: OOD detection and OOD generalization
- Neuron activation patterns and limits of prior neuron-based work
- Formulating neuron activation states and neuron activation coverage (NAC)
- Application 1: OOD detection (NAC-UE)
- Application 2: OOD generalization (NAC-ME)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- InD assumption
  - ML advances assume training and test data share a distribution = in-distribution (InD) (cite)
  - rarely holds in real world: out-of-distribution (OOD) data, e.g. samples from unseen classes (cite)
  - OOD/InD shifts challenge well-trained models, big performance drops (cite)
- Two avenues
  - OOD detection: tools telling InD from OOD inputs, avoid unreliable predictions (cite)
  - OOD generalization: robust networks generalizing to unseen OOD data, trained only on InD (cite)
  - many studies, but still arguable on fundamental cause and mitigation of OOD issues (cite)
- Neuron behavior
  - neurons show distinct activation patterns for InD vs OOD inputs (cite) (Figure 4)
  - potential: characterize model status w.r.t. OOD via neuron behavior
  - prior work modifies networks (cite) or lacks a suitable definition of activation states (cite)
    - neuron truncation clipping outputs to separate InD/OOD, better detection (cite); but lower classification ability (cite)
    - threshold -> binary states (activated or not) from neuron output (cite) (cite); discards distribution details
  - ours: natural activation states + simple statistical property of neuron distribution
- Neuron activation state + NAC
  - state from neuron output + influence on model decisions
  - influence = gradients of KL divergence (cite) between network output and uniform vector, inspired by (cite)
  - coverage analysis in system testing (cite): neurons rarely activated (covered) by training set can trigger undetected bugs, e.g. misclassifications, at test
  - neuron activation coverage (NAC): coverage degree of neuron states under InD training data (Figure 2)
    - frequently activated by InD training inputs -> higher coverage score -> fewer underlying defects
  - applied to two OOD tasks
- OOD detection
  - OOD data trigger abnormal activations -> smaller coverage scores than InD test data (Figure 2)
  - NAC-UE (Uncertainty Estimation): average coverage scores over all neurons = data uncertainty
  - CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k; new SOTA vs 21 previous best OOD detection methods
  - CIFAR-100: 10.60% better FPR95, 4.58% gain AUROC vs ViM (cite) (Figure 1)
- OOD generalization
  - underlying defects can exist outside the coverage area (cite) -> hypothesis: larger coverage, more robust network
  - NAC-ME (Model Evaluation): robustness by integrating coverage distribution of all neurons
  - DomainBed (cite): positive NAC-generalization correlation across architectures and datasets
  - vs InD validation criteria: picks more robust models, stronger correlation with OOD test performance
  - Vit-b16 (cite): 11.61% better rank correlation with OOD test accuracy

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in machine learning systems depend on an implicit assumption that the training data and the test data come from the same distribution, which is called in-distribution (InD). But this assumption rarely holds in real-world scenarios because of out-of-distribution (OOD) data, e.g., samples from unseen classes. These distribution shifts between OOD and InD are often a big challenge for well-trained models and lead to significant drops in performance.

Previous work on this OOD problem mainly comes from two directions: 1) OOD detection and 2) OOD generalization. OOD detection is about designing tools that can tell InD and OOD data inputs apart, so that unreliable model predictions are not used. OOD generalization, on the other hand, is about developing robust networks that generalize to unseen OOD data while only using InD data for training. There are many studies, but it has been shown that existing approaches are still arguable when it comes to giving insights into the fundamental cause and mitigation of OOD issues.

As suggested by previous studies, neurons can show distinct activation patterns when they are exposed to data inputs from InD and from OOD (See Figure 4). This shows that there is potential in using neuron behavior to characterize the model status with respect to the OOD problem. Several studies do recognize this, but they either choose to modify the neural networks, or they do not have a suitable definition of neuron activation states. For example, one method proposes a neuron truncation strategy that clips the neuron output to separate the InD and OOD data, which improves OOD detection. But this truncation unexpectedly decreases the classification ability of the model. More recently, one work and another work use a threshold to put neurons into binary states (i.e., activated or not) based on the neuron output. However, this characterization throws away valuable details of the neuron distribution. Different from them, in this paper we show that by using natural neuron activation states, a simple statistical property of the neuron distribution can effectively help the OOD solutions.

  - neuron activation coverage (NAC): coverage degree of neuron states under InD training data (Figure 2)
    - frequently activated by InD training inputs -> higher coverage score -> fewer underlying defects
  - applied to two OOD tasks

- OOD detection

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in machine learning systems depend on an implicit assumption that the training data and the test data come from the same distribution, which is called in-distribution (InD). But this assumption rarely holds in real-world scenarios because of out-of-distribution (OOD) data, e.g., samples from unseen classes. These distribution shifts between OOD and InD are often a big challenge for well-trained models and lead to significant drops in performance.

Previous work on this OOD problem mainly comes from two directions: 1) OOD detection and 2) OOD generalization. OOD detection is about designing tools that can tell InD and OOD data inputs apart, so that unreliable model predictions are not used. OOD generalization, on the other hand, is about developing robust networks that generalize to unseen OOD data while only using InD data for training. There are many studies, but it has been shown that existing approaches are still arguable when it comes to giving insights into the fundamental cause and mitigation of OOD issues.

As suggested by previous studies, neurons can show distinct activation patterns when they are exposed to data inputs from InD and from OOD (See Figure 4). This shows that there is potential in using neuron behavior to characterize the model status with respect to the OOD problem. Several studies do recognize this, but they either choose to modify the neural networks, or they do not have a suitable definition of neuron activation states. For example, one method proposes a neuron truncation strategy that clips the neuron output to separate the InD and OOD data, which improves OOD detection. But this truncation unexpectedly decreases the classification ability of the model. More recently, one work and another work use a threshold to put neurons into binary states (i.e., activated or not) based on the neuron output. However, this characterization throws away valuable details of the neuron distribution. Different from them, in this paper we show that by using natural neuron activation states, a simple statistical property of the neuron distribution can effectively help the OOD solutions.

We first propose to formulate the neuron activation state by looking at both the neuron output and its influence on model decisions. Specifically, inspired by earlier work, we model the neuron influence as the gradients from the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the network output and a uniform vector. Next, to characterize the relationship between neuron behavior and OOD issues, we take insights from coverage analysis in system testing, which shows that neurons that are rarely activated (covered) by a training set can potentially trigger undetected bugs, such as misclassifications, at test time. With this in mind we introduce the concept of neuron activation coverage (NAC), which quantifies how much the neuron states are covered under InD training data (See Figure 2). In particular, if a neuron state is often activated by InD training inputs, NAC gives it a higher coverage score, which indicates fewer underlying defects in this state. In this paper NAC is applied to two OOD tasks:

OOD detection. OOD data can trigger abnormal neuron activations, so they should get smaller coverage scores than the InD test data (Figure 2). So we present NAC for Uncertainty Estimation (NAC-UE), which simply averages the coverage scores over all neurons and uses this as the data uncertainty. We evaluate NAC-UE on three benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k), and it sets new state-of-the-art performance compared to the 21 previous best OOD detection methods. In particular, NAC-UE gets a 10.60% improvement on FPR95 (and a 4.58% gain on AUROC) over CIFAR-100 compared to the competitive ViM (See Figure 1).

OOD generalization. Since underlying defects can exist outside of the coverage area, our hypothesis is that the network becomes more robust when the coverage area is larger. For this we use NAC for Model Evaluation (NAC-ME), which measures how robust a model is by integrating the coverage distribution of all neurons. In experiments on DomainBed, we find that NAC and model generalization ability are positively correlated, and this holds consistently across architectures and datasets. Also, compared to InD validation criteria, NAC-ME selects more robust models and also has a stronger correlation with OOD test performance. For example, on the Vit-b16, NAC-ME is better than validation criteria by 11.61% in terms of rank correlation with OOD test accuracy.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in machine learning systems hinge on an implicit assumption that training and test data share the same distribution, known as in-distribution (InD) [1,2,3,4]. However, this assumption rarely holds in real-world scenarios due to the presence of out-of-distribution (OOD) data, e.g., samples from unseen classes [5]. Such distribution shifts between OOD and InD often pose a drastic challenge to well-trained models, leading to significant performance drops [6,7].

Prior efforts to tackle this OOD problem mainly follow two avenues: 1) OOD detection and 2) OOD generalization. The former aims at designing tools that differentiate between InD and OOD data inputs, thereby refraining from using unreliable model predictions [8,9,10,11]. In contrast, OOD generalization focuses on developing robust networks that generalize to unseen OOD data while relying solely on InD data for training [5,12,13,14,15]. Despite numerous studies, it has been shown that existing approaches are still arguable in providing insights into the fundamental cause and mitigation of OOD issues [16,17].

As suggested by [16,18], neurons can exhibit distinct activation patterns when exposed to data inputs from InD and OOD (See Figure 4), revealing the potential of leveraging neuron behavior to characterize model status with respect to the OOD problem. Yet, although several studies recognize this, they either modify the neural networks [16] or lack a suitable definition of neuron activation states [18,19]. For instance, [16] proposes a neuron truncation strategy that clips neuron output to separate InD and OOD data, improving OOD detection; however, such truncation unexpectedly decreases the model's classification ability [20]. More recently, [18] and [19] employ a threshold to characterize neurons into binary states (i.e., activated or not) based on the neuron output, a characterization that discards valuable details of the neuron distribution. Unlike them, in this paper we show that by leveraging natural neuron activation states, a simple statistical property of the neuron distribution can effectively facilitate OOD solutions.

We first propose to formulate the neuron activation state by considering both the neuron output and its influence on model decisions. Specifically, inspired by [11], we model neuron influence as the gradients derived from the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [21] between the network output and a uniform vector. Then, to characterize the relationship between neuron behavior and OOD issues, we draw on coverage analysis in system testing [22,23], which reveals that neurons rarely activated (covered) by a training set can potentially trigger undetected bugs, such as misclassifications, during testing. In this sense, we introduce the concept of neuron activation coverage (NAC), which quantifies the coverage degree of neuron states under InD training data (See Figure 2). In particular, if a neuron state is frequently activated by InD training inputs, NAC assigns it a higher coverage score, indicating fewer underlying defects in this state. We apply NAC to two OOD tasks:

OOD detection. Since OOD data potentially trigger abnormal neuron activations, they should present smaller coverage scores than InD test data (Figure 2). We therefore present NAC for Uncertainty Estimation (NAC-UE), which directly averages coverage scores over all neurons as data uncertainty. We evaluate NAC-UE on three benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1k), where it establishes new state-of-the-art performance over the 21 previous best OOD detection methods. Notably, NAC-UE achieves a 10.60% improvement on FPR95 (with a 4.58% gain on AUROC) over CIFAR-100 compared to the competitive ViM [24] (See Figure 1).

OOD generalization. Given that underlying defects can exist outside the coverage area [22], we hypothesize that network robustness increases with a larger coverage area. To this end, we employ NAC for Model Evaluation (NAC-ME), which measures model robustness by integrating the coverage distribution of all neurons. Through experiments on DomainBed [17], we find that a positive correlation between NAC and model generalization ability consistently holds across architectures and datasets. Moreover, compared to InD validation criteria, NAC-ME not only selects more robust models but also correlates more strongly with OOD test performance. For instance, on the Vit-b16 [1], NAC-ME outperforms validation criteria by 11.61% in terms of rank correlation with OOD test accuracy.
